day.text: Drew: Owl eggs go to the Owl's target, which is me. My nest is +0, so either someone else visited me, which I have no record of, or Blair's Owl didn't visit me at all. Blair, which one is it? Casey and Finley's visit to Ellis still contradicts Casey's 0, and that's the clearest lie I see.
day.note: Owl eggs go to the Owl's target, which is me, so my +0 means someone else visited me or Blair didn't visit me. I can't name another visitor, so I'll say so and keep pressure on Blair.
Everything I can say has been said. I'll stay quiet this beat and save my argument for the vote.

day.text: Ellis: Casey's zero-visitor read clashes with Finley's visit, and Casey hasn't answered the round 1 role question. I'm with Finley and Drew on Casey.
day.note: Casey's Eagle reading of zero visitors conflicts with Finley's visit, and Finley and Drew are both pressing Casey. I'll join the Casey throw to keep the table aligned.

day.text: Alex: Casey's zero-visitor Eagle read contradicts Finley's visit, and Casey hasn't answered the role question. I'm throwing at Casey.
day.note: Finley, Ellis, and Drew all point at Casey, whose Eagle read contradicts Finley's visit. I'll back Casey as the throw.

day.text: Blair: Casey's zero read clashes with Finley's visit, and Casey still hasn't answered. I'm with the table, throwing at Casey. CAW.
day.note: Casey is Farm, so the table going after Casey is good for us. I'll back the throw and push the vote.

day.text: Drew: Casey's zero read clashes with Finley's visit, and Casey still hasn't answered the round 1 role question. I'm throwing at Casey too.
day.note: Casey's zero-visitor claim clashes with Finley's visit and Casey hasn't answered the role question, so I'll go with the table and throw at Casey.

day.text: CAW. Casey's Eagle read is the only one that contradicts a real visit. Let's vote.
day.note: I'm Farm this round and the table is converging on Casey, whose zero-visitor claim contradicts my real visit. Calling CAW to move to the vote.

Alex.note: Finley and Casey were both Farm, so the Meowfia are among Blair, Drew, and Ellis. I'll visit Drew with my Hawk to test whether Drew is Meowfia.

Blair.note: I'm the Sphinx this round, and the farm roles in play are Eagle, Falcon, Hawk, and Tit. I'll visit whoever holds the Eagle, which lets me find a Farm player and learn their identity.

Casey.note: As Eagle I gain an egg per visitor to my target, so I'll visit Ellis, who has been the most suspicious.

Drew.note: As Farm Falcon, I'll visit Blair, who has been consistent so far, to learn who they visited.

Ellis.note: I'm Meowfia Floofer again. Drew leads the scores and has been probing me, so I'll hug Drew to block their night action.

Finley.note: As the Tit I'll test a role guess. Ellis's Owl report matched a real Floofer visit, so I'll visit Ellis and guess Owl.

Alex.feeling: Round 3 is messy: the claims conflict everywhere, and I'm not confident about who is lying, though Casey's Eagle read looks the most suspicious.

Blair.feeling: Tense: I'm the Meowfia Sphinx, the table is about to eggsecute Casey, who is actually Farm, and I'm not sure who my partner is.

Casey.feeling: Tense and muddled: the claims contradict each other, and I'm the one being voted on, so I'm relying on my Eagle read.

Drew.feeling: Messy and contradictory: several role claims conflict, and I'm unsure whether Casey or Blair is lying, so I'm voting on the clearest contradiction.

Ellis.feeling: Tense and messy: the table is split over contradictory Eagle, Owl, and Tit reads, and I'm trying to steer suspicion toward Casey while staying believable as a Kookaburra.

Finley.feeling: Tense but workable: the table is converging on Casey, and Casey's zero-visitor read clashes with my real Tit visit to Ellis.

Alex.note: Casey is the consensus target. I'll throw my Wild, which is worth 0 if banked, so it adds a vote at little cost.

Blair.note: Casey is Farm, so eggsecuting Casey wins the round for Meowfia. I'll throw two low cards at Casey to make sure they lead the vote.

Casey.note: Finley's visit to Ellis contradicts my Eagle read of zero visitors, so Finley is most likely Meowfia. I'll throw at Finley with my wild and a low card, keeping my high cards.

Drew.note: The table is converging on Casey, so I'll throw one low card at Casey and keep my higher cards.

Ellis.note: The table is converging on Casey. I'll add one Wild vote at Casey, which costs nothing if Meowfia wins and returns my highest card if Casey is Meowfia.

Finley.note: Casey is the table's consensus target and my read agrees. I'll throw two low cards at Casey to add votes and keep my high cards.

Alex.confusing: The Eagle rule was hard to read: the card says it counts visitors to the Eagle itself, but several players argued it counted visitors to the target. The Owl's egg condition was also easy to misread.
Alex.fun: Round 2 was fun because the table tried to untangle conflicting Falcon, Owl, and Eagle reports, and the Floofer claim turned out to be the lie that everyone chased.
Alex.change: I would make the dawn reports more explicit about who visited whom, since much of the day went to guessing whose story was true.
Alex.regret: In round 1 I threw at Finley, a Farm player, and let Ellis's Owl story pass without challenge. I should have pressed Ellis, who was actually Meowfia, and checked Ellis's visit claims against Blair's +0 more carefully.

Blair.confusing: The Eagle and Owl wording caused most of the table's arguments: players disagreed about whether Eagle counts visitors to itself or to its target, and whether an Owl egg goes to the Owl or the target. Those disputes drove the day discussions more than the actual roles did.
Blair.fun: As the Sphinx in round 3, I learned Casey was the Eagle and watched the table throw at a Farm player while I stayed hidden. Winning the round by eggsecuting a Farm player was satisfying.
Blair.change: I would make the Eagle and Owl text unambiguous, with explicit examples of who gains eggs and when. I would also show each player's throw totals in the eggsecution reveal, since the values stay hidden.
Blair.regret: In round 1 I threw at Finley, a Farm player, and followed the table instead of pressing Ellis, whose Pigeon-to-Owl flip was the real Meowfia tell. I would have thrown at Ellis, which might have flipped the round to Farm.

Casey.confusing: The Tit rule was easy to misread. In round 2 I guessed Owl on Ellis, who really was the Owl, so my +1 was my own correct guess, and I didn't realize that until the reveal.
Casey.fun: Round 2's day was a chain of contradicting Eagle, Owl, and Falcon stories, and I enjoyed working out which claims could fit the card text.
Casey.change: I'd make the dawn reports clearer about whether a role's guess or visit was correct, since the Tit's +1 looked like a mystery to everyone.
Casey.regret: In round 2 I told the table Ellis was not an Owl, which was false. I should have said my guess had landed and asked for the +1 to be explained by my own visit, and I would not have been accused.

Drew.confusing: The Floofer's hug rule and how a Floofer visit shows up in an Owl or Eagle report were hard to track, so I couldn't tell whether my own +0 or +2 readings were reliable.
Drew.fun: Round 1's day, when the table traded Eagle and Owl claims and I got to see Finley's and Ellis's stories fall apart under cross-checking.
Drew.change: I'd make the dawn reports for confused players clearer about which parts are wrong, so a confused player can still reason from their own result.
Drew.regret: In round 2 I voted with the table to throw at Casey, a Farm player, while Finley was the Floofer, so I should have pressed harder on the Finley and Ellis contradictions instead of following the majority.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle and Owl egg rules were hard to read, since people disagreed about whether an Eagle's gain counts visitors to itself or to its target. Several players also misread the Owl's no-visitor condition.
Ellis.fun: Round 3's vote, where the table converged on Casey and the Meowfia side won by a clear 7-2 throw count, felt like a real read on the table's logic.
Ellis.change: I would make the dawn reports and visit logs more explicit, such as stating exactly which visitors counted toward each egg change, so claims could be checked.
Ellis.regret: In round 1 I claimed Pigeon, then flipped to Owl after Blair's +0, which made me look like a liar; I should have stuck to one role and explained the mismatch from the start. In round 2, as Farm, I piled onto Casey, who was also Farm, without enough evidence, which cost my side the round.

Finley.confusing: The Eagle and Owl egg rules were hard to parse from the card text alone, and Alex and Drew argued the Eagle rule wrong in round 1. Confusion over whose visitors count cost the table a lot of time.
Finley.fun: Round 2 was fun because I was Meowfia and had to lie low while Farm players fought over Casey's unexplained egg.
Finley.change: I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so players don't argue over whether a visit counts for the target or the actor.
Finley.regret: In round 3 I helped eggsecute Casey, who was Farm, and my team lost that round. I should have questioned Blair's Hawk/Owl stories more, since Blair was the Meowfia Sphinx.

review.title: Three Wrong Eggsecutions
review.headline: The table eggsecuted a Farm player three rounds running; Meowfia cashed in.
review.summary: Every vote landed on a Farm player, so Meowfia won all three rounds. Round 1 turned on an argument over how the Eagle works. Round 2 turned on an unexplained +1 egg. In round 3 Blair, a Meowfia Sphinx, threw two low cards at Casey and banked 8 points, jumping from 5 to 13 and winning the game. Several true pieces of evidence were dismissed or misread.

rounds.recap: Ellis, the Floofer, claimed Pigeon and then switched to Owl when Blair's +0 exposed it. The table ignored that and went after Finley, a real Eagle. Alex and Drew misread the Eagle card, and Finley was eggsecuted as Farm.

Finley, the Floofer, hugged Drew. Ellis's Owl truthfully learned that a Floofer visited Drew, but Drew's +0 made it look like a lie. Casey had a +1 that nobody could explain, and the whole table threw at Casey, a Farm Tit. Casey's +1 most likely came from a Pigeon visit that was never claimed.

Blair, the Sphinx, learned the Eagle was Casey. Ellis, the Floofer, hugged Drew, which pushed Finley, Casey and Drew into confusing claims about visits. Casey's honest Eagle read of 0 clashed with Finley's Tit claim, so the table piled onto Casey. Meowfia won, and Blair banked 8 points with a cheap throw.

highlights.text: Ellis flipped from Pigeon to Owl once Blair's +0 broke the claim, and the table accepted it and moved on.
Ellis truthfully reported that a Floofer visited Drew, and Drew's +0 under a hug made the truth look like a lie.
Casey's +1 egg had no source anyone could name, and it got Casey eggsecuted.
Blair, the Sphinx, threw two 4s at Casey and banked 8 points, which won the whole game.

confusions.what: Said the Eagle gains eggs only for visitors to the Eagle. The card says visitors to the target.
Agreed with Alex's wrong Eagle reading and repeated it against Ellis and Finley.
Backed the wrong Eagle reading and threw at Finley, the real Eagle.
Said Eagles gain only from visits to themselves and threw at Finley.
Said a Tit lays only on a correct guess and then called the +1 unexplained. Casey's reasoning was right, but Casey could not tell that someone else had visited, and the table took it as guilt.
Said Drew's +0 as Eagle meant no Floofer visited. Drew was hugged, so the Eagle did nothing, and Drew did not realize it.
Took Drew's +0 as proof that nobody visited Drew, ignoring that the hug blocks the Eagle.
Took an Eagle read of 0 as proof that Ellis had no visitors. Casey was hugged, so the Eagle did nothing.
Treated a Falcon visit that gave no egg as proof that Blair visited someone, though Drew was hugged. Drew also expected an Owl egg to land in Drew's own nest.
As the Owl bluff, said no egg came because nobody else visited Drew, which is backwards. Alex caught it.
Said Drew's +0 did not rule out another visitor to Drew, then used that to defend Blair's Owl. This misread how the Owl egg works.

worked: The hug effect created good false evidence. A hugged Eagle or Falcon sees nothing and reports zero, which looks like a lie to everyone else.
Owl reports of visiting animals were true and useful, and the Floofer hit in round 2 was a good puzzle.
Throw size as a signal: Blair's cheap two-card throw in round 3 turned a Meowfia win into a score jump.
problems: Hugged roles get no warning that they were hugged. A hugged Eagle, Falcon or Tit looks identical to one with nothing to report, so honest Farm claims look false. Tell hugged players at dawn, or let them learn they were blocked.

Meowfia won all three rounds because the table fixated on one contradiction and never checked the Floofer, who was in plain sight. Farm has too little reliable evidence to find the cat, and Meowfia face almost no pressure.
The Eagle card wording ('visitors they had') was misread by three players. Clarify that the Eagle gains for visitors to its target, or word it explicitly.
Unexplained eggs, like Casey's +1, cannot be traced and get treated as proof of guilt. Consider telling a player their egg count came from a visit, or limiting these effects.

Throwing a cheap card at the winning side's target pays out the full value of the winner's best throw. Blair banked 8 with two 4s, which is a runaway lead, and the bank rewards a Meowfia win far more than a Farm win.
